title: Christ the King
hook: the year's last Sunday, instituted in 1925

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dedication of the Lateran, the pope's own cathedral. Your line was the mother church. What small thing did you do for yours? Day six hundred eighty-eight.

December 1925. Europe is seven years out of a world war that toppled emperors and kings. New movements are promising that the nation, or the party, or the leader, deserves everything. In Rome, Pope Pius XI publishes a letter announcing a brand-new feast, one of the youngest on the calendar. Its name sounds old-fashioned, even then: Christ the King. Today it's the last Sunday of the Church's year, the week before Advent starts again.
screen: `1925: KINGS FALLEN, NEW POWERS RISING.` → `A NEW FEAST.` → `THE YEAR'S LAST SUNDAY.`

segments.voice: Pius XI's letter, Quas Primas, argued that many of the world's troubles came from pushing Christ out of public life, and that people needed reminding whose kingdom outlasts all the others. At first the feast fell on the last Sunday of October. After the Second Vatican Council it moved to the last Sunday of the liturgical year, so the year now ends looking toward the end of all things. But here's the twist the feast is built on. Which king? The Gospels give Jesus the title king almost only during his passion. Before Pilate, Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "My kingdom is not of this world." The soldiers dress him in purple and crown him with thorns as a joke. And the sign nailed above his head, in three languages, says: "THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS." Rome meant it as mockery, a warning to anyone who claimed a crown. Christians took it as the truest thing anyone said that day. In one year of the cycle, the Gospel for this feast is that exact scene: Jesus on the cross, the sign above him, and a criminal beside him asking, Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom. In another, it's the sheep and the goats: the king who says, whatever you did for the least of these, you did for me. So the crown is thorns, the throne is a cross, and the king is found in the hungry and the prisoner. Catholics call him king, and then look at how he reigns.
screen: `QUAS PRIMAS, 1925.` · `MOVED TO THE YEAR'S LAST SUNDAY.` · `MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.` · `A CROWN OF THORNS, A CROSS.` · then, large: `THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask who rules your time. Open your calendar, or think back over this past week. Where did your hours actually go? Work, screens, worry, people, sleep. Don't judge it; just look. Then ask a plain question: who or what is in charge of my time? If you pray, you can offer next week's hours to Christ. If you don't, choose one hour next week that you'll give to something that matters to you. The bell holds the time.
Christ the King. The last Sunday of the Church's year, created by Pius XI in 1925, honoring a king whose crown was thorns. Today's word.
Your line: king on a cross. Today, when someone powerful is in the news, remember the sign over the cross, and what kind of king it named. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate the solemnity of Our Lord Jesus Christ, King of the Universe, on the last Sunday of the liturgical year, the Sunday before Advent; some parishes hold a Eucharistic procession or a holy hour.

what it means: a king whose crown was thorns and whose throne was a cross, found in the least of these.
what a scholar hears: Quas Primas (1925) answering the rise of nationalism and secularism; moved in 1969 to close the liturgical year.

notes: Quas Primas, 11 December 1925; originally the last Sunday of October; moved in the 1969 calendar to the last Sunday in Ordinary Time. Confirm.
Lectionary: Year A Matthew 25:31–46; Year B John 18:33–37; Year C Luke 23:35–43. Confirm.
Luke 23:38 Douay-Rheims: the inscription text; confirm exact capitalization/wording.

Rome's crucifixion of Jesus framed explicitly; the sign as Roman mockery.
